rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The anbūnī form elides the imperative hamza as a dialectal or phonological variant, with no change in meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamza elision: anbiʾūnī → anbūnī — drops the hamza in the imperative, dialectal/phonological variant.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isrāʾīla has a variant treatment of hamza among the ten canonical readings; no semantic difference is stated.
rows.anchor: Hamza treatment variant within ten canonical readings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some ten-reader traditions retain the yāʾ of the object pronoun in the full form fa-rhabūnī.
rows.anchor: Yāʾ retained (full form) — some ten-reader traditions preserve the object pronoun yāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ḍamma on hāʾ is a canonical vowel-harmony variant of the kasra form and does not alter meaning.
rows.anchor: Ḍamma on hāʾ instead of kasra — canonical variant; dialectal vowel harmony difference; no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra on mīm is a canonical case-vowel variant of the ḍamma form, varying in pause or connection without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Kasra on mīm instead of ḍamma — canonical variant; case vowel variation in pause/connection; no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamzated nabīʾīn reading derives the word from informing rather than elevation, making the etymological distinction explicit.
rows.anchor: explicitly from n-b-ʾ (to inform) — the hamza-form anchors the etymology to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn for ṣād reading is a canonical letter substitution with no semantic difference, only a shift from emphatic to plain sibilant.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with sīn instead of ṣād — ibdāl (letter substitution); no semantic change, phonetic variation between emphatic ṣ and plain s

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām blends ṣād toward zāy, producing an intermediate articulation without a difference in meaning.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with ishmām (blending ṣ toward z sound) — intermediate articulation between ṣād and zāy; phonetic but no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raʾuf form has a shorter vowel pattern than raʾūf, slightly reducing intensity while remaining intensive.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant: shortened vowel pattern raʾuf instead of raʾūf — faʿul instead of faʿūl; slightly less intensive form but still within the intensive register

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿusura reading changes internal vowels but retains the abstract sense of hardship.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel variant changes internal voweling but preserves the abstract hardship meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maysuratin is a canonical vowel variant without a major semantic shift.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel variant maysuratin (maysuratin), with no major semantic shift

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form V tāʾ assimilates into ṣād, a phonetic compression with no change in meaning.
rows.anchor: Canonical assimilation of Form V tāʾ into ṣād, phonetic compression without semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An active reading means that people return, shifting agency toward volitional return rather than divine compulsion.
rows.anchor: shifts agency from divine compulsion to volitional return; canonical reading in some qira'at traditions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamzated nubūʾa derives from n-b-ʾ, informing, rather than n-b-w, elevation, making the etymological fork phonologically explicit.
rows.anchor: deriving from n-b-ʾ (to inform) rather than n-b-w (to elevate) — etymological fork made phonologically explicit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I taʿlamūna means you know or learn, unlike Form II tuʿallimūna, you teach; the variant shifts the agents from teachers to learners.
rows.anchor: shifts agents from teachers to learners; changes the epistemic relationship entirely

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive reading says a prophet was killed, so the ribbiyyūn continued after his death rather than fighting alongside him.
rows.anchor: ribbiyyūn continued AFTER the prophet's death, not alongside him in battle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person ya-prefix changes direct address, you shall clarify, into reported speech, they shall clarify, recasting the covenant as narration.
rows.anchor: changes the covenant from dialogue to narration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person yaktumūnahu reading means they do not conceal it and aligns with the narrated-speech version of tubayyinunnahu.
rows.anchor: matches the 3rd-person variant of tubayyinunnahu, maintaining consistency in the narrated-speech reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kasra on sīn is an alternate canonical Form I vowel pattern; both fatḥa and kasra readings are canonical.
rows.anchor: Kasra on sīn — alternate Form I voweling (faʿila pattern); both fatḥa and kasra readings canonical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person masculine reading makes alladhīna the subject rather than the object: those who rejoice are the ones who think themselves safe.
rows.anchor: 3rd person masculine — alladhīna becomes subject not object

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person reading with kasra combines the two variant dimensions.
rows.anchor: 3rd person + kasra — combines both variant dimensions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra on sīn is the same canonical vowel variant noted for the second word, also found among the seven readings.
rows.anchor: Kasra on sīn — same vowel variant as word 2; canonical in seven readings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person reading with kasra and ḍamma means let him not suppose them, shifting the addressee.
rows.anchor: 3rd person + kasra + ḍamma

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of tāʾ into sīn shortens tatasāʾalūna to tassāʾalūna without changing the Form VI meaning.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of tāʾ into sīn: tatasāʾalūna → tassāʾalūna — phonological simplification, same Form VI meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive arḥāmi is governed by the implied bi in bihi, making the wombs objects of oath or invocation alongside God.
rows.anchor: wombs become objects of oath/invocation alongside God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This liaison variant places ḍamma on the wāw of aw before hamzat waṣl and leaves meaning unchanged.
rows.anchor: Ḍamma on wāw of aw before hamzat waṣl — phonetic liaison variant; no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second liaison variant puts ḍamma on both the nūn of an and the wāw of aw, without semantic shift.
rows.anchor: double liaison variant; no semantic shift

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative qalīlan parses adverbially, as ḥāl or mafʿūl muṭlaq, rather than as a nominative substitute, shifting the sense from except a few to except slightly.
rows.anchor: as adverbial accusative (ḥāl or mafʿūl muṭlaq) rather than nominative substitute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn reading for ṣād reflects dialectal variation between Tamīm and Quraysh, with the same meaning but a softer sound.
rows.anchor: reflects dialectal variation (Tamīm vs. Quraysh); semantically identical but phonetically softer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām pronounces ṣād with a trace of zāy, an intermediate articulation preserving both dialectal registers.
rows.anchor: intermediate articulation between ṣ and s, preserving both dialectal registers simultaneously

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sīn variant realizes ṣād as plain sīn, losing emphasis but not changing meaning.
rows.anchor: no semantic change but phonetically loses the emphatic quality

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām blends ṣād with a trace of zāy, an intermediate dialectal pronunciation.
rows.anchor: a blended sound between ṣ and z); reflects a dialectal intermediary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Ḥafṣ reading is the Form IV jussive of ḥ-l-l, meaning do not make lawful or dissolve the sanctity of.
rows.anchor: Form IV jussive of ḥ-l-l — do not make-lawful / do not dissolve the sanctity of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruḍwān, with ḍamma on rāʾ, and riḍwān, with kasra, are valid forms of the same maṣdar without a meaning difference.
rows.anchor: both are valid Forms of the same maṣdar with no meaning difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on nūn gives the lighter shanʾān form; the heavier shanaʾān also means hatred and may differ in intensity.
rows.anchor: both mean hatred with possible intensity difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading in makes the clause conditional, if they barred you, rather than an, that they barred you, moving from fact to hypothesis.
rows.anchor: changes temporal frame from established fact to hypothetical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of tāʾ adds tashdīd initially but is phonological only, with no semantic difference.
rows.anchor: phonological variant only, no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the liaison reading, the final lām of hal takes ḍamma before the hamza in unabbiʾukum, smoothing the phonetics.
rows.anchor: Liaison reading where hal's final lām gets ḍamma before hamza of unabbiʾukum -- phonetic smoothing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿabuda form is read as a noun meaning slave or devoted one, with ṭāghūt genitive; this shifts the construction from verb to nominal.
rows.anchor: shifts from verb to nominal:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iḍāfa reading makes jazāʾ govern mithli in the genitive, framing it as recompense of the equivalent and tightening the equivalence.
rows.anchor: making the equivalence tighter than the adjective reading

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iḍāfa reading changes mithlu from a nominative adjective describing jazāʾ to a genitive muḍāf ilayhi governed by it.
rows.anchor: changing mithlu from describing jazāʾ to being governed by it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the iḍāfa reading, kaffāra governs ṭaʿām in the genitive, making feeding the definition of the expiation.
rows.anchor: making feeding the definition of the expiation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form II intensifies opening: multiple canonical readers read fattaḥnā as we flung wide open.
rows.anchor: intensifies the act of opening; multiple canonical readers attest this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The -āhu variant keeps Form X but uses masculine agreement instead of feminine plural agreement with shayāṭīn, potentially suggesting one agent.
rows.anchor: removes feminine plural agreement with shayāṭīn, potentially suggesting a single agent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both wajhiya with fatḥa and wajhī without it occur as canonical seven-reader variants.
rows.anchor: both wajhiya (with fatḥa) and wajhī (without) are canonical seven-reader variants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sīn replaces ṣād, removing emphasis and reflecting dialectal variation in the sibilant.
rows.anchor: removes emphatic quality; reflects dialectal variation in pronunciation of the sibilant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām gives ṣād partial zāy quality, intermediate between emphatic and plain sibilants.
rows.anchor: partial zāy quality — intermediate between emphatic and plain sibilant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard iqtadih includes hāʾ al-sakt, a purely phonetic pause marker with no semantic content.
rows.anchor: the hāʾ is purely phonetic, marking a stop without semantic content

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another canonical variant drops hāʾ al-sakt, leaving a bare imperative without a pausal marker.
rows.anchor: Variant dropping the hāʾ al-sakt entirely — bare imperative, no pausal marker

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With kasra, hāʾ is treated as a pronoun rather than a pausal hāʾ, making follow him or it explicit.
rows.anchor: Variant with kasra on the hāʾ — hāʾ read as a pronoun (him/it)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A long kasra treats hāʾ as a pronoun with elongation, emphasizing its pronominal reference.
rows.anchor: pronoun hāʾ with elongation, emphasizing the pronominal reference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possessive suffix yāʾ may be pronounced with fatḥa rather than sukūn, a purely phonological variant without semantic change.
rows.anchor: no semantic change, purely phonological variant of prosodic openness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sīn replaces emphatic ṣād through dialectal variation, preserving the same word and meaning.
rows.anchor: same word, phonological variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām gives ṣād a trace of zāy coloring, a phonetic intermediate between ṣirāṭ and zirāṭ.
rows.anchor: a phonetic intermediate between ṣirāṭ and zirāṭ attested in Quranic recitation traditions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qayyiman is an intensive adjective emphasizing permanence and self-subsistence, unlike qiyaman as a verbal noun; it shifts the sense from upright to perpetually self-sustaining.
rows.anchor: qayyim emphasizes permanence and self-subsistence (al-qayyūm = the self-subsisting, divine attribute)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibrāhāma is a variant vocalization associated with some Hijazi Quranic manuscripts; it is dialectal or orthographic and does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: this form is associated with some Hijazi Quranic manuscripts; no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibdāl substitutes sīn for ṣād; sīn is described as etymologically expected from Latin strata, with ṣād an Arabized emphatic substitution.
rows.anchor: sīn is the etymologically expected consonant (from Latin strata), ṣād is an arabicized emphatic substitution

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām blends ṣād and zāy, retaining emphasis while hinting at zāy; Qunbul and Khalaf attest this reading.
rows.anchor: preserving emphatic quality while hinting at the zāy variant, attested in Qunbul and Khalaf readings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Form IV imperfect indicative presents sending the winds as ongoing divine action.
rows.anchor: ongoing divine action of sending winds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular rīḥ replaces plural riyāḥ, shifting from multiple beneficial winds to one wind entity.
rows.anchor: shifts from multiple beneficial winds to a single wind entity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dotting variant gives n-sh-r, spreading or scattering, and describes winds as spreading agents rather than heralds.
rows.anchor: n-sh-r = spreading, scattering, resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, nashran is an active verbal noun of n-sh-r, depicting winds as actively spreading.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift to fatḥa: active verbal noun of n-sh-r

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nushuran is a plural of nashūr or nashūra, presenting winds as multiple spreading or reviving agents.
rows.anchor: winds as multiple agents of revival

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contracted mayt can mean already dead, while full mayyit can mean destined to die; the reading shifts the land's death from process to state.
rows.anchor: The variant shifts the land's death from process to state

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Full assimilation of tāʾ into dhāl produces a heavier consonant cluster that emphasizes the effort of remembering.
rows.anchor: heavier consonant cluster emphasizes the effort of remembering

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I suggests individual killing, whereas Form II suggests systematic massacre, a contrast between execution and extermination.
rows.anchor: Form I = individual killing, Form II = systematic massacre.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical variant opens the possessive yāʾ with fatḥa, a pronunciation change without semantic effect.
rows.anchor: open pronunciation of the first-person pronoun suffix, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra in ummi is the regular genitive of iḍāfa rather than vocative fatḥa, giving son of my mother.
rows.anchor: genitive by iḍāfa instead of vocative fatḥa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second segment likewise identifies ummi with kasra as the standard genitive in iḍāfa.
rows.anchor: standard genitive in iḍāfa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural dhurriyyāt makes offspring groups explicitly multiple rather than collective singular.
rows.anchor: emphasizing multiplicity of distinct offspring groups

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third-person plural yāʾ replaces second-person tāʾ, changing the excuse-makers from the addressed audience to reported third parties.
rows.anchor: changes the excuse-makers from the addressed audience to a reported third party

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person plural shifts the covenant's addressees from direct participants to reported third parties who might claim their ancestors were idolaters.
rows.anchor: changing the addressee of the covenant from direct participants to reported third parties

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form I yalḥadūna means incline or dig laterally, while Form IV yulḥidūna means cause deviation or commit ilḥād; the first foregrounds physical action and the second causative abstraction.
rows.anchor: Form I foregrounds the physical action; Form IV foregrounds the causative-abstract meaning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The short raʾuf variant and standard raʾūf are both canonical; the shorter form may reflect dialect or rhetorical compression.
rows.anchor: both canonical (within the Seven); shorter form may be dialectal or rhetorical compression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive kulli is construct state with zawjayni, meaning from every pair of two rather than every kind, two pairs.
rows.anchor: reads as construct state (iḍāfa) with zawjayni

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading applies imāla to the alif, tilting fatḥa toward kasra on rāʾ as a dialectal phonetic feature.
rows.anchor: Imāla of the alif — tilting fatḥa toward kasra on the rāʾ, dialectal phonetic feature
